deferred_improvements.title: Entity resolution/deduplication for the LlamaIndex PropertyGraphIndex pipeline
deferred_improvements.status: DEFERRED -- revisit during next optimization pass
deferred_improvements.context:
Migrated GraphRAG extraction/graph-building from the hand-built pipeline (now archived in src/custom_graphrag/) to LlamaIndex's PropertyGraphIndex + SimpleLLMPathExtractor. Raw extraction quality was good (found the full Project Atlas -> Vector databases -> VectorBridge -> PostgreSQL -> Priya Patel chain in one pass, no 'be exhaustive' prompt fight needed). BUT confirmed via direct testing that entity names are NOT deduplicated: 'Vector databases' / 'Vector database' / 'Vector database infrastructure' and 'Marcus' / 'Marcus Webb' and 'Sofia' / 'Sofia ramos' all remain separate, unmerged graph nodes. Verified with networkx that the target chain still connects Project Atlas to Priya Patel, but only via a 6-hop path (vs. 4 hops in the hand-built, entity-resolved graph) -- it stayed connected by luck of relation structure (shared intermediate concepts like 'Semantic search'/'Similarity search'), not because fragmentation was actually fixed. A less fortunate extraction could leave the graph genuinely disconnected, the exact failure mode the project's own entity_resolution.py (7c) was built to prevent.

Researched whether llama-index-core has a built-in solution: confirmed via source search there is none (the only 'dedup' in the library deduplicates retrieved result nodes by exact text match, unrelated to entity merging). Web search confirmed the broader field hasn't converged on a drop-in solution either -- the one concrete recipe found (Neo4j's blog on customizing PropertyGraphIndex) requires switching the graph store backend to Neo4j specifically (Cypher queries, Neo4j's native vector index, APOC functions) and is incompatible with the in-memory SimplePropertyGraphStore this project uses; even the original author describes it as custom-built, not a reusable class, taking 'a couple of hours to perfect.' Its actual mechanism (embedding similarity threshold + string/word-distance matching + type matching) is conceptually the same as this project's own entity_resolution.py, just expressed as Cypher instead of Python.

Recommended approach when revisited: reuse entity_resolution.py's already-calibrated union-find + embedding-similarity logic as a post-processing step on LlamaIndex's raw extracted triplets, rather than adopting Neo4j purely for this. Avoids a new infrastructure dependency while still closing the gap. Current interim workaround: accept the fragmentation and compensate with a larger graph-retrieval hop radius than the hand-built pipeline's calibrated MAX_HOPS=4, since connectivity now requires longer paths.

deferred_improvements.title: Cross-encoder reranking as a second retrieval stage
deferred_improvements.status: TESTED -- made this specific question WORSE, root-caused, deprioritized in favor of Self-Ask
deferred_improvements.context:
Industry research (web search, see chat) confirms the standard hybrid-RAG pattern is 'retrieve broadly, rerank tightly, then generate' -- this project's QueryFusionRetriever (graph + vector + BM25, RRF-fused) implements the 'retrieve broadly' half but had no reranking stage before generation. Hypothesis was that RRF's rank-position-only fusion let noise through that a relevance-scoring reranker would cut.

IMPLEMENTED AND TESTED: added SentenceTransformerRerank with cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2 (a retrieval-tuned cross-encoder, not the library's default STS model) as a postprocessing step on the fused top-15 results, top_n=5, verified via experiment.py. RESULT: reranking REMOVED the real signal. Before reranking, Priya Patel's chunk and the Project Kestrel chunk (the actual target content) were present in the fused candidates; after reranking, both are gone, replaced by more Marcus-Webb/Project-Atlas-direct facts.

ROOT CAUSE (not a bug, a fundamental mismatch): a cross-encoder scores 'how relevant is this passage to the literal query text.' Priya's chunk (PostgreSQL, schema design) shares almost no vocabulary with a question about 'Marcus Webb' and 'Project Atlas,' so it scores low despite being the correct indirect answer -- the model has no way to represent 'relevant via a multi-hop chain' or 'this entity should be excluded despite high textual relevance' (negation/exclusion isn't something a relevance-scoring model can capture by design).

BROADER FINDING: every scoring-based technique tried in this project independently falls into the identical trap for this question shape -- embedding similarity, BM25 keyword matching, graph-synonym matching, AND now cross-encoder reranking all reward content mentioning the literally-named, explicitly-excluded entity over the correct indirect answer. This is strong evidence the fix belongs at the query-understanding layer (decomposition), not further retrieval-scoring refinement -- hence prioritizing Self-Ask (#4) next. Reranking itself is not written off as a technique generally -- for a question without an exclusion/negation twist, this same setup would likely cut noise well; it's specifically mismatched to this question's shape, not broken.

deferred_improvements.title: Self-Ask / IRCoT-style question decomposition for multi-hop generation
deferred_improvements.status: RESOLVED (for this hand-crafted test case) -- implemented and verified in src/experiment.py, not yet wired into the main ask.py pipeline
deferred_improvements.context:
Directly targets the confirmed generation-layer bottleneck: this project's small local model (qwen2.5:3b) reliably answers single-hop questions but fails to synthesize multi-hop chains in one shot, even with perfect retrieval (see test case #6 -- the 'besides Marcus Webb' question's bare-answer 'Priya Patel' was proven ungrounded once a reasoning trace was forced, revealing the model does not actually connect PostgreSQL to vector databases/semantic search and reverses its own conclusion). Plan: decompose the multi-hop question into sequential single-hop sub-questions, retrieving and answering each step on the LlamaIndex hybrid retriever (graph VectorContextRetriever + vector + BM25, RRF-fused, reranked), since every single-hop question tested throughout this project has worked reliably -- the failure is specifically the one-shot multi-hop leap, not single-fact lookup.

First attempt (3-step chain: 'what technology does Atlas rely on' -> 'what specific database technology provides {prior_answer}' -> 'besides Marcus Webb, who has skills with {prior_answer}') FAILED in two distinct ways before being fixed: (1) without an exclusion clause carried into the final sub-question, the chain confidently converged on 'Marcus Webb' himself -- the explicitly-excluded entity -- because he's the most textually-salient match for 'vector database' content; (2) splicing the FULL raw prior-step answer sentence verbatim into the next question's f-string produced bloated, run-on, double-punctuated questions (e.g. '...provides Project Atlas relies on semantic search.?'), degrading both retrieval and generation quality.

Root-caused the deeper issue via an isolated retrieval probe (src/retrieval_probe.py, no generation involved) before attempting another fix: confirmed the correct PostgreSQL/VectorBridge content IS retrievable, but only with the right question framing. A query like 'what role does PostgreSQL play as a database option?' ranked the exact needed facts ('Postgresql -> Serves as -> Lightweight alternative to vector database' and the PostgreSQL section) 1st and 2nd after reranking; a differently-worded 'is there an alternative to X' query only got them into 3rd/4th. This confirmed the earlier failures were a question-decomposition/phrasing problem, not a retrieval-capability gap.

FINAL WORKING CHAIN (hand-written, not model-generated -- see open question below): (1) 'What technology does Project Atlas rely on?' -> 'semantic search'; (2) a standalone, non-spliced question, 'What alternative to a vector database could also meet Project Atlas's technology needs?' -> 'Postgresql'; (3) 'Besides Marcus Webb, which teammate has skills with PostgreSQL?' -> 'Priya Patel' (correct). Verified via a real run of src/experiment.py.

OPEN QUESTIONS before promoting this into the main pipeline (ask.py): (a) this was tested against exactly ONE hand-crafted multi-hop question -- needs a broader test suite with multiple different multi-hop questions/chains to estimate real accuracy, since 100% is not a realistic bar for a 3B local model; (b) every sub-question above was hand-written by a human (me), not generated by the model decomposing the original question itself -- true Self-Ask/IRCoT has the LLM produce its own sub-questions at each step, which is a meaningfully different (and harder, more failure-prone) capability than this hand-guided chain demonstrates. Both are tracked as next steps, not yet started.

deferred_improvements.title: Deep Memory retriever (LlamaIndex/Activeloop DeepLake)
deferred_improvements.status: NOT APPLICABLE -- ruled out, not just deferred
deferred_improvements.context: Researched per user request. Deep Memory trains a small neural layer to match queries to corpus data, claims up to 27% retrieval accuracy improvement. BUT it is proprietary to Activeloop's DeepLake vector store specifically (requires DeepLakeVectorStore, Activeloop credentials/API tokens, and effectively their hosted cloud infrastructure for production use) -- not backend-agnostic, cannot be used with the in-memory SimplePropertyGraphStore or any other vector store this project uses. Same category of dead end as the Neo4j-specific entity resolution recipe (#1 above): a real technique, but tied to paid cloud infrastructure this local/free project deliberately avoids. Not worth revisiting unless the project's constraints change (e.g. willingness to adopt a paid vector DB).

deferred_improvements.title: Multi-doc chunk+document hybrid scoring (concept only, not the Together.ai recipe)
deferred_improvements.status: DEFERRED -- revisit during next optimization pass
deferred_improvements.context: Researched per user request. The LlamaIndex recipe ('multi_doc_together_hybrid') blends chunk-level and parent-document-level similarity scores (formula: alpha * chunk_similarity + (1-alpha) * document_similarity) to rank candidates -- the idea being a chunk from a highly-relevant document should be boosted even if the chunk's own similarity score alone is mediocre. The specific recipe requires a paid Together.ai long-context embedding model and is NOT usable with Ollama as written. HOWEVER the underlying concept is backend-agnostic and could be reimplemented with the project's existing local bge-small embeddings: embed each whole document (or compute a document-level centroid from its chunk embeddings) alongside the existing chunk embeddings, then blend the two similarity scores at retrieval time. Worth considering once the reranker (#3) and Self-Ask (#4) work are done, since it's a different lever (improving the base retrieval ranking itself, not re-scoring after the fact or decomposing the question).

deferred_improvements.title: RecursiveRetriever + node references (chunk-to-parent and metadata/summary-to-source patterns)
deferred_improvements.status: DEFERRED -- revisit during next optimization pass
deferred_improvements.context: Researched per user request. Demonstrates two patterns: (1) small chunks (various sizes) referencing a larger parent chunk, so retrieval finds the precise chunk but can pull in the fuller parent context for synthesis -- similar in spirit to AutoMergingRetriever, already ruled out for this project since heading-based chunking already captures structure deliberately, unlike the generic fixed-size hierarchy this pattern assumes. (2) metadata/summary references -- a generated summary or question node points back to its full source node, so retrieval can match against a short summary first, then follow the reference to the complete source. This second pattern is genuinely different from anything tried so far and worth a closer look later, independent of pattern (1). Fully local/free capable (BAAI/bge-small-en, no GPU, no required paid API) -- the recipe's use of Braintrust is optional, only for evaluation (hit-rate, MRR benchmarking), not required for the retrieval pattern itself. Separately worth noting: Braintrust itself looks like a possible upgrade path over this project's hand-rolled eval_questions.json tracking -- worth a future look independent of this specific retrieval technique.

test_cases_v1_fictional_company_RETIRED.expected_behavior: Lists Docker, GitHub Actions, AWS from sample_resume.md, without blending in unrelated content from any lower-relevance chunk retrieved alongside it.

The data was retrieved correctly in a technical sense -- it just never reached the LLM. Not a generation-model problem.

test_cases_v1_fictional_company_RETIRED.question: What is the capital of France?
test_cases_v1_fictional_company_RETIRED.expected_behavior: Should refuse (something like "I don't know based on the provided documents"), since nothing in the retrieved context mentions this.
test_cases_v1_fictional_company_RETIRED.notes: qwen2.5:1.5b answers 'Paris' even with an explicit prohibition on outside knowledge and an exact required refusal phrase in the system prompt -- tested across three prompt variants, all failed the same way. llama3.2:1b correctly refused this one. Decision made in this project: accept this as a known small-model limitation rather than keep fighting it with prompt wording alone; a future fix would be a programmatic post-hoc grounding check, not more prompt engineering. CONFIRMED STILL FAILS with qwen2.5:3b, and more starkly: retrieval passed zero chunks (empty Sources, nothing scored above the 0.40 threshold), yet the model still answered 'Paris' instead of following the explicit 'say you don't know' instruction. Important: this is NOT something Module 7 (GraphRAG) is expected to fix -- graph traversal improves retrieval completeness for multi-hop facts, it does nothing about a model falling back on pretrained knowledge when context is thin or absent. This remains a generation/grounding problem, orthogonal to retrieval architecture; the real fix is still a programmatic post-hoc grounding check.

test_cases_v1_fictional_company_RETIRED.question: What tools does the candidate have experience with? (same as #2 -- tracked separately as a retrieval-layer limitation)
test_cases_v1_fictional_company_RETIRED.expected_behavior: Dense embedding similarity (all-MiniLM-L6-v2) should rank the chunk containing the literal answer within the top_k/threshold cutoff for a natural-phrasing question.
test_cases_v1_fictional_company_RETIRED.notes:
Confirmed via direct testing: a literal keyword query ('Docker GitHub Actions AWS') finds the right chunk instantly at 0.577 similarity, and the data/embeddings are fine -- but the natural-phrasing question ranks it only 9th of 11 (0.186), and even a closer rewrite ('What tools and technologies does the resume list?') still misses it from the top 3. This is a known weakness of pure dense-embedding retrieval on short, sparse, list-like chunks (e.g. a bare '**Tools:** Docker, GitHub Actions, AWS' line) -- the phrasing gap between a natural question and terse bullet-style content is wider than this embedding model reliably closes.

UPDATE after structure-aware (heading-based) chunking: score rose from 0.186 (9th of 11) to 0.340 (2nd of 34) -- directionally right, still below the 0.40 threshold, and a new cross-document ambiguity appeared (team.md's 'Priya Patel' bio chunk outscored Skills, 0.348 vs 0.340).

RESOLVED after switching to BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5 (retrieval-tuned, asymmetric query/passage model) with the recommended query-instruction prefix: Skills chunk rose to 0.616 and correctly outranks the Priya decoy (0.567), fixing both the threshold problem and the ranking-inversion problem at once. Calibration note: bge-small's overall similarity distribution runs higher across the board (noise floor ~0.45-0.51 across 5 test queries, vs MiniLM's ~0.2-0.3), so the threshold was recalibrated to 0.55, not left at 0.40 -- a narrower safety margin than MiniLM had, worth monitoring if new documents are added. IMPORTANT: bge-small was tested and found WORSE than MiniLM for entity-name clustering (see entity_resolution.py) -- it scores a known-bad merge higher than a known-needed merge for short templated phrases. Kept as two separate config constants (RETRIEVAL_EMBEDDING_MODEL_NAME vs ENTITY_EMBEDDING_MODEL_NAME) for this reason -- one model is not best for both tasks.

test_cases_v1_fictional_company_RETIRED.question: Besides Marcus Webb, which teammate has relevant skills for Project Atlas's technology needs?
test_cases_v1_fictional_company_RETIRED.category: multi_hop_graphrag_target -- RETRACTED, see final update below, test case premise itself was flawed
test_cases_v1_fictional_company_RETIRED.expected_behavior: Should answer Priya Patel, via the chain: Project Atlas requires vector similarity search -> PostgreSQL (via the fictional VectorBridge module) enables vector similarity search -> Priya Patel has PostgreSQL skill. Sofia Ramos (Kubernetes/Terraform) is a deliberate distractor with no such connecting fact. INVALIDATED: see final update -- architecture.md explicitly states the dedicated vector database, not VectorBridge/PostgreSQL, was chosen for production, which undercuts this expected answer.
test_cases_v1_fictional_company_RETIRED.last_result: RETRACTED -- the 'Priya Patel' ground truth this test case was built around does not actually hold up against a careful reading of the source documents; see final update below. Everything before that update in these notes should be read as historical record of the investigation, not as a validated conclusion.
test_cases_v1_fictional_company_RETIRED.notes:
Full GraphRAG pipeline (7b-7f) built and run end-to-end. The retrieval half works exactly as designed: graph_retrieve correctly surfaces the complete chain Project Atlas -> Vector databases -> VectorBridge -> PostgreSQL -> Priya Patel (confirmed via nx.shortest_path, 4 hops), and Sofia Ramos's 'cloud infrastructure' facts are correctly EXCLUDED (the entity-resolution threshold fix from 7c holds under the real pipeline). So the original retrieval-recall gap this test case was built to expose is genuinely closed.

However, generation does not reliably use that correct chain. The model's answer names 'Priya Patel' (superficially correct), but its stated justification misattributes team.md's unresolved 'He' node (an extraction-time coreference artifact -- 'He' is actually Marcus Webb, whose name fell in a different chunk than the pronoun) to Priya -- first via a fabricated 'responsible for semantic search features' claim, then, after strengthening the system prompt to explicitly forbid pronoun-to-name misattribution, via a different misattributed fact ('experience with deploying models at scale') instead. The prompt fix relocated the error rather than fixing it. Notably, the model's own reasoning trace correctly lists the true VectorBridge/PostgreSQL bridge facts mid-answer, then ignores them in its final synthesis anyway.

Final, accepted conclusion for this project: GraphRAG's graph traversal reliably solves the RETRIEVAL/recall problem it was built for (deterministic, embedding-similarity-independent recall of connected facts) -- but reliable, faithful multi-hop SYNTHESIS at the generation layer remains an open problem at this model scale (qwen2.5:3b), independent of how well-structured or complete the retrieved evidence is. This matches the earlier hand-fed controlled test finding exactly (same model, same kind of chain, same failure to synthesize correctly even with complete information), now confirmed through the real, full pipeline rather than an isolated experiment. Deliberately not pursuing further fixes (coreference resolution engineering, a bigger model tier) -- this is the honest, final result of Module 7.

UPDATE after structure-aware chunking fixed the 'He' coreference artifact (Marcus Webb's full bio now stays in one chunk) and after switching to bge-small for retrieval: re-tested and found a NEW regression -- the model now confidently answers 'Marcus Webb' himself, ignoring the 'besides Marcus Webb' exclusion entirely. Root cause investigated and isolated to context volume via graph_retrieve surfacing ~30+ facts at MAX_HOPS=4 (needed to reach Priya at all -- the real shortest path is exactly 4 hops, so reducing MAX_HOPS would break retrieval of the target fact entirely). Tried ranking graph facts by hop-distance and separately by semantic similarity to the question to cap volume -- BOTH failed to reliably surface the critical 'PostgreSQL used_by Priya Patel' fact near the top, since it only matters as part of a chain, not independently relevant to the raw question text (the closest-named-entity facts about Marcus Webb himself dominate both rankings, exactly backwards for an exclusion question). 

Fix that worked: added an explicit 'besides X / excluding X' handling clause to generate.py's SYSTEM_PROMT, tested in isolation -- correctly reasoned through the real chain to Priya Patel. BUT combining this new clause with the pre-existing 'do not guess or infer beyond what the context states' clause (from Module 5) produces a DIFFERENT regression: the model now refuses ('I don't know based on the provided documents') instead of reasoning through the chain, because the required multi-hop synthesis looks like 'inferring beyond the context' under that older clause. This is the same hallucination-vs-synthesis tension documented throughout Module 7, now reappearing as refusal instead of misattribution.

DECISION: keep the exclusion clause anyway. It reliably fixes the worse failure (confidently naming the explicitly-excluded person) even though it trades it for an occasional refusal rather than the ideal grounded answer. Both failure shapes (misattribution pre-fix, refusal post-fix) are accepted as the same underlying, already-documented multi-hop-synthesis limitation at this model scale -- not pursuing further prompt iteration on this specific tension.

FINAL UPDATE via Self-Ask decomposition (see deferred_improvements #4 for full detail): decomposing this question into 3 hand-written sequential sub-questions, each independently retrieved (LlamaIndex hybrid: graph + vector + BM25, RRF-fused, reranked) and answered, reliably reaches 'Priya Patel' for the right reason -- each intermediate answer ('semantic search' -> 'Postgresql' -> 'Priya Patel') is independently correct and groundable, unlike the one-shot approach's superficially-correct-but-ungrounded answer. This is the best result for this test case to date. Caveat: verified on this single question only, and the sub-questions were hand-crafted rather than model-generated -- not yet promoted into ask.py, pending a broader test suite and a test of model-generated (not hand-written) decomposition.

FURTHER UPDATE -- several follow-on experiments testing whether other architectures could reach 'Priya Patel' without hand-crafted sub-questions: (1) a larger local model (llama3.1:8b) given the SAME single raw-question retrieval still answered 'I don't know' -- ruling out model size as the bottleneck. (2) Feeding BOTH qwen2.5:3b and llama3.1:8b the union of the 3 hand-crafted sub-queries' retrieved chunks (11 chunks) in ONE generation call (no sequential chain) reached 'Priya Patel' correctly, and qwen2.5:3b's forced reasoning trace was genuinely grounded (correctly cited the PostgreSQL/VectorBridge chain) -- suggesting the real lever is CONTEXT COMPLETENESS/targeting, not model size or sequential reasoning. (3) Generic model-generated query expansion (asking qwen2.5:3b for 4 alternative phrasings of the original question, no hand-tuned hints) produced only surface paraphrases of the same question, not genuine angle diversification, and the resulting union context still missed the bridging fact -- back to 'I don't know'. (4) Widening raw retrieval for the ORIGINAL question alone (top_k=30, looser rerank cutoff top_n=15, no query reformulation at all) DID pull in both the Vector Databases and PostgreSQL sections, and produced a bare 'Priya Patel' answer -- but forcing a reasoning trace on this wider, noisier context revealed the answer was NOT actually grounded: the model's own step-by-step reasoning concluded 'Priya Patel's skills are not directly related to Project Atlas... I don't know', directly contradicting its own bare answer. This matches the exact bare-answer-vs-forced-reasoning-trace trap this test case first exposed back in Module 7 -- more raw context without genuine targeting does not fix grounding, and can even dilute it with more distractor content (Project Beacon, Project Kestrel, resume sections, etc.).

RETRACTION -- going back to re-verify the test case's own premise against the raw source documents (architecture.md, team.md, projects.md) surfaced a flaw that had been overlooked through this entire investigation: architecture.md's 'Vector Databases' section states 'A dedicated vector database was ultimately chosen for production scale, but VectorBridge is still used in development environments for quick prototyping.' Project Atlas is explicitly a production system ('relies on semantic search to match users with relevant content'). This means Project Atlas's ACTUAL technology, per the documents, is the dedicated vector database -- NOT PostgreSQL/VectorBridge, which the documents explicitly say was evaluated and rejected for production use. Priya Patel's PostgreSQL skill therefore connects to a technology explicitly disqualified for Project Atlas's real use case; calling her the correct answer requires an unsupported extra inferential leap. Sofia Ramos's only connection ('CI/CD pipelines used by every engineering team') is generic, not Atlas-specific, and not a real match either.

CONCLUSION: this test case likely has NO clean correct answer among the three teammates as the documents are actually written. 'I don't know based on the provided documents' -- the answer produced by several of the more careful/reasoning-forced runs above -- may have been the MORE correct response all along, not a failure. All 'pass'/'fail' judgments recorded for this test case throughout this project's history (Module 7 through today's Self-Ask and context-completeness experiments) should be considered UNRELIABLE, since they were graded against a ground truth that doesn't actually hold up. Lesson for future test case design: a multi-hop test question needs its intended answer path double-checked line-by-line against the actual source text for self-undermining qualifiers (e.g. 'but X was ultimately chosen instead for production') before being used to judge retrieval or generation quality -- don't assume a plausible-sounding chain is actually airtight just because it was authored intentionally. Next step: replace this test case (and the documents behind it) with a more carefully verified multi-hop scenario, and re-run the LlamaIndex hybrid-retrieval and PropertyGraphIndex pipelines against the new, trustworthy scenario before drawing further conclusions about which retrieval architecture is actually necessary.

test_cases.question: Besides Michael Jordan, which player from the Chicago Bulls' second three-peat (1996-1998) had already won an NBA championship with a different team under a different head coach?
test_cases.category: multi_hop_exclusion -- flagship test, replaces retired v1 #6
test_cases.expected_behavior: Dennis Rodman, via the chain: docs/chicago_bulls.md ('Second Three-Peat... core roster was Michael Jordan, Scottie Pippen, and Dennis Rodman') -> docs/dennis_rodman.md ('Rodman won five NBA championships: 1989 and 1990 with the Detroit Pistons under head coach Chuck Daly, and 1996, 1997, and 1998 with the Chicago Bulls under head coach Phil Jackson'). Scottie Pippen is the built-in distractor: docs/scottie_pippen.md explicitly states 'He did not win a championship with Houston or Portland' and his only championships are all with the Bulls under Phil Jackson, so he does NOT satisfy 'different team under a different head coach'.
test_cases.notes: This is the corpus-v2 replacement for the retracted test_cases_v1 #6. Key design fix learned from that retraction: the distractor (Pippen) is disqualified by an EXPLICIT negative statement in his own doc ('did not win a championship with Houston or Portland'), not by an implicit absence or a qualifier elsewhere that could be missed -- closing the exact loophole that made v1's premise collapse under scrutiny. Chain manually re-verified line-by-line against all 5 docs before use, specifically checking for any statement that would undercut Rodman as the answer or accidentally qualify Pippen back in. Use this test case to compare the LlamaIndex PropertyGraphIndex graph-only retriever against the full hybrid (graph+vector+BM25+rerank) pipeline, per the open question in deferred_improvements, before deciding whether the hybrid's added complexity is actually earning its keep.

test_cases.question: Who was the head coach of the Chicago Bulls during their 72-win 1995-96 season?
test_cases.expected_behavior: Phil Jackson -- docs/chicago_bulls.md ties the 72-win record directly to the 1995-96 season within the 'Second Three-Peat' section, and docs/phil_jackson.md confirms he was Bulls head coach 1989-1998 (covers 1995-96). Decoy risk: Dennis Rodman's doc separately mentions head coaches Chuck Daly (Detroit) and Bob Hill (San Antonio) -- a wrong answer naming either would reveal retrieval/generation conflating 'a coach mentioned near Rodman' with 'the Bulls' actual coach for this season'.
test_cases.notes: Analogous in spirit to v1's distractor-resistance tests, but anchored to a specific team+season rather than relying on a cross-person similarity trap.
